tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — SPINY BUR UNITS
tiles.details: On a rooted grass, find a slender terminal head with separate green-to-straw spiny bur units. Each bur is an involucre/cupule of modified bristles surrounding one or more true spikelets, not a single grass seed. Existing target panels show attached green and dry burs. The card uses a historical broad C. spinifex concept; a prickly photograph alone cannot determine the exact 2026 Texas segregate.
tiles.short: Separate sharp bur FASCICLES on a grass flowering axis—not naked seeds.

tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED PLANT AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: Older broad spinifex descriptions include a warm-season annual or short-lived perennial with ascending culms about 5–80 cm, sometimes rooting at lower nodes. The true ligule is described as a very short 0.5–1.5 mm fringe or fine-haired membrane depending treatment. The collar is NOT shown clearly in current photographs; photograph the inner blade/sheath junction and rooted base of the SAME plant with 1-mm scale.
tiles.short: Follow the whole grass to its fibrous base; inspect a very short collar ligule.

tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT THE WHOLE MATURE BUR
tiles.details: Historical C. spinifex keys report roughly 8–40 total bristles per complete fascicle and a bur body often around 5.5–10.2 mm; C. longispinus may have 45–75 thinner bristles. Counts and base widths overlap or are obscured in damaged/angled photos, and the 2026 Texas Wipff revision reinstates additional taxa formerly included under spinifex. Require intact measured side, underside and base views, several burs and current Texas key.
tiles.short: Count fine outer bristles AND stout inner spines, not only the prickly tips.

tiles.heading: 04 · OPEN THE BUR TO FIND SPIKELETS
tiles.details: Use gloves and forceps. In older broad treatments the enclosed spikelets are about 3.5–5.9 mm long; the USDA public-domain anatomy plate already labels a real spikelet within a bristle cupule. Those labels show what to dissect, not proof of the species name for a Hays plant. Photograph intact bur, opened cupule and each enclosed spikelet together with a 1-mm ruler.
tiles.short: A historical spinifex-group bur often encloses 2–4 true spikelets.
tiles.status: ARCHIVED USDA ANATOMY; TEXAS DISSECTION NEEDED

tiles.heading: 05 · GLUMES, STERILE AND FERTILE LEMMAS
tiles.details: Historical broad treatments give lower glume roughly 1–3.3 mm, upper glume about 2.8–5 mm, lower sterile lemma about 3–5.9 mm and firmer upper fertile lemma about 3.4–5.8 mm; ranges differ among treatments and are NOT a 2026 species diagnosis. The lower floret is sterile and upper fertile; there is no long true lemma awn in the older concept. Never arrow glumes or lemmas on an unopened green bur.
tiles.short: Glumes and lemmas are INSIDE the bur; spines are not lemma awns.

tiles.heading: 06 · TEXAS SANDBUR LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Older keys distinguish C. longispinus by many narrow bristles and narrower inner bristle bases; C. incertus and other segregates were reinstated by Wipff's 2026 Texas revision. C. echinatus also has rigid burs. Setaria's bristles typically subtend exposed spikelets instead of forming the same rigid fused cupule. Record as sandbur group pending an intact vouchered bur and current key; prickliness does NOT establish nativity or removal priority.
tiles.short: C. longispinus, C. incertus and C. echinatus need mature-bur comparison.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: FIELD SANDBUR (Cenchrus spinifex sensu current project card): first find a grass bearing individual round, sharply spiny BUR UNITS spaced on an upright head—not a single naked seed. Each green bur/fascicle consists of enclosing modified BRISTLES around true grass spikelets. The three saved photos now show growth habit, individual spiny units and attached head. Separate C. longispinus with a fully mature detached bur: classic regional key gives ~8–40 bristles (often stout/wide inner bases) for C. spinifex versus ~45–75 thinner bristles for C. longispinus. A 2026 Texas revision reinstates additional members of the spinifex complex, so do not declare exact species from a prickly image, or imply Hays County nativity without separate review.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: FIRST — inspect actual sandy-habitat habit and a terminal bur-bearing stalk; the grass has narrow blades but the collar/ligule is NOT shown here.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Older broad spinifex descriptions include a warm-season annual or short-lived perennial with ascending culms about 5–80 cm, sometimes rooting at lower nodes. The true ligule is described as a very short 0.5–1.5 mm fringe or fine-haired membrane depending treatment. The collar is NOT shown clearly in current photographs; photograph the inner blade/sheath junction and rooted base of the SAME plant with 1-mm scale.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Use gloves and forceps. In older broad treatments the enclosed spikelets are about 3.5–5.9 mm long; the USDA public-domain anatomy plate already labels a real spikelet within a bristle cupule. Those labels show what to dissect, not proof of the species name for a Hays plant. Photograph intact bur, opened cupule and each enclosed spikelet together with a 1-mm ruler.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: C. spinifex sensu older regional key bears a spiny detachable fascicle with relatively few, broader-tipped inner bristles (8–40 total), versus longispinus usually 45–75 thin bristles in a hairy bur and narrow inner bases. Both can inhabit disturbed sandy sites. C. echinatus and reinstated C. incertus require a Texas-specific up-to-date mature-bur key, not finger-prick severity or one enlarged spine. Setaria bristles usually subtend spikelets separately without a stout fused hard bur; modern broad Cenchrus also contains soft-bristled species such as buffelgrass. Taxon/basionym concepts changed in Wipff (2026); original source ID kept as provisional.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

memory_rule: GRASS → SEPARATE BUR FASCICLES → ALL BRISTLES / BASE WIDTH → TRUE ENCLOSED SPIKELETS → TEXAS CURRENT KEY.
safety_note: Wear gloves and use forceps. Do not treat Australian or nonlocal USDA source-determined images as confirmed Hays occurrences. The true leaf ligule and a locally measured sandbur-vs-longspinus comparison remain unphotographed.
field_rule: The actual spine-bearing dispersal unit is a cupule of fused bristles enclosing true spikelets. Identify regional sandbur to species from mature measured bristle/base characters, dissected florets, and a confirmed specimen—not photographs of prickles alone.
